text:
Based on the text, Harringay went into his studio about **ten o'clock**.

This is stated in the second paragraph: "Following his version of the affair, the narrative deposes that Harringay went into his studio about ten o'clock to see what he could make of the head that he had been working at the day before."
D'après le texte, Harringay entre dans son atelier vers **dix heures** (« about ten o'clock »).

Based on the text, Harringay loaded his brush with **vermilion** (or bright red) by mistake.

The relevant passage states: "The eye, then? Catastrophe! he had filled his brush with **vermilion** instead of brown, and yet he had felt sure it was brown!"

Harringay a chargé son pinceau de **vermillon** (vermilion) par erreur, au lieu du brun.

Le texte indique explicitement : *"Catastrophe! he had filled his brush with vermilion instead of brown..."*
Based on the text, the dimensions of the canvas are **24 by 20**, and it is enamelled a **pale green** (specifically described as "Hedge Sparrow's Egg Tint").

D'après le texte, la toile qu'Harringay présente comme preuve a les dimensions de **24 par 20** (les unités ne sont pas précisées, mais il s'agit probablement de pouces ou de centimètres) et elle est émaillée d'une couleur **vert pâle** (décrite dans le texte comme « Hedge Sparrow's Egg Tint », soit une teinte rappelant l'œuf de moineau des haies, qui est un vert pâle).

Le passage pertinent est :
> « He supports it by a small canvas (24 by 20) enamelled a pale green... »
"That was rather hasty of you," said the picture.
« That was rather hasty of you, » said the picture.

An artist named Harringay becomes frustrated with his lifeless painting of an Italian organ-grinder, which suddenly comes to life and offers him masterpieces in exchange for his soul. Harringay rejects the devil’s bargain and violently paints over the canvas with enamel, silencing the creature and leaving behind only a blank, green panel.

L'artiste R.M. Harringay, insatisfait de son tableau d'un joueur d'orgue de barbarie, assiste avec effroi à l'animation diabolique de la toile qui lui reproche son manque d'inspiration et lui propose un pacte en échange de chefs-d'œuvre. Pour se débarrasser de l'entité, Harringay recouvre le tableau de peinture verte, mais l'histoire se termine sur une note sceptique, suggérant que cet incident n'est qu'une invention de l'artiste pour justifier son incapacité à produire une œuvre majeure.

Based on the text, Pawkins published his work on the mesoblast of the Death's Head Moth in **1891**.

This is stated in the paragraph beginning: "But in 1891 Pawkins, whose health had been bad for some time, published some work upon the 'mesoblast' of the Death's Head Moth."

D'après le texte, Pawkins publie son travail sur le mésoblaste du sphinx tête-de-mort en **1891**.

Le passage concerné indique : « But in 1891 Pawkins, whose health had been bad for some time, published some work upon the "mesoblast" of the Death's Head Moth. »

Based on the text, Hapley first noticed the strange moth on the **third day** of his study of diatoms.

The text states: "It was on the third day of the diatoms that Hapley became aware of a novel addition to the local fauna."

D'après le texte, Hapley remarque l'étrange papillon le **troisième jour** de son étude des diatomées.

Le passage pertinent indique : « It was on the third day of the diatoms that Hapley became aware of a novel addition to the local fauna. » (C'est le troisième jour des diatomées qu'Hapley a pris conscience d'une nouvelle addition à la faune locale.)

Based on the text, at the end of the story, Hapley is spending the remainder of his days in a **padded room** (in an asylum).

He says the moth is the **ghost of Pawkins**.

À la fin de l'histoire, Hapley passe le reste de ses jours dans une **chambre matelassée** (ou asile d'aliénés), où il est gardé sous contrainte.

Concernant le papillon (ou mite), il affirme qu'il s'agit de **l'ombre (ou fantôme) de Pawkins**. Il le considère donc comme un spécimen unique et méritant d'être capturé.
"The eye of faith is no better than the eye of science," said Hapley, awkwardly.
Hapley was thunderstruck. He gasped. The Vicar was staring at him. Clearly the man saw nothing. "The eye of faith is no better than the eye of science," said Hapley, awkwardly.

Driven to madness by the death of his lifelong scientific rival, Professor Pawkins, the entomologist Hapley becomes obsessed with catching a mysterious moth that only he can see, interpreting it as a manifestation of his deceased enemy. His relentless pursuit of this hallucination leads to public humiliation and physical injury, ultimately resulting in his confinement in an asylum where he remains tormented by the phantom insect.

Après avoir provoqué la mort de son rival scientifique, l'entomologiste Hapley sombre dans la folie et est hanté par une hallucination persistante d'un papillon inconnu, qu'il associe à l'esprit de son défunt adversaire. Il finit ses jours enfermé dans un asile psychiatrique, tourmenté par cette créature invisible qu'il s'obstine à vouloir capturer.
